title: Why were Victorian elites so effective? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Works in Progress argues Victorian Britain's elites, educated for character and team spirit, networking nightly during the London Season, succeeded by forming a unified high-trust 'village' (Gemeinschaft) rather than through STEM rigor or long working hours.

insights.claim: Elite Victorian schooling was oddly progressive: classics took at least half of teaching hours, science was resisted, classroom time was modest, and sports could fill ten to twenty hours a week.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Counterexample to the view that elite success needs STEM-heavy, hours-heavy education.

insights.claim: Victorian public schools sent boys to board by about age eight, and student self-government via prefects was designed to teach leadership, helping produce an elite with no strong subnational loyalties.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Early shared peer formation built elite cohesion and loyalty.

insights.claim: Eton alone supplied about 30% of nineteenth-century cabinet ministers and 40% of prime ministers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Illustrates extreme concentration of elite formation in a few institutions.

insights.claim: Oxbridge admitted almost every applicant, most students in the early Victorian period took easy 'pass' degrees, and only 8.1% of honors degrees in 1855–60 and 13.7% in 1910–14 went to science students.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Elite formation prioritized moral and social training over technical skill.

themes.theme: Soft skills and networking as work

insights.claim: Elite Victorians spent only about four or five hours a day on clear office work, but balls, dinners and clubs gave access to information on jobs, investments and secret political decisions, effectively fusing personal and professional life.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Dense in-person networking can be a productive substitute for long working hours.
insights.quote: access to a vast information network: information about jobs, investment possibilities, secret political decisions

insights.claim: For about five months a year the elite congregated in Mayfair and Belgravia, within half an hour's walk of one another, in the London Season that coincided with Parliament, mixing political networking with matchmaking.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag

insights.claim: Society balls functioned as both teenage house party and business networking convention, mixing ages and sexes, which was unlike many segregated events.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Social settings that mix generations and functions expand network reach.
insights.quote: it was both a teenage house party and a business networking convention

insights.claim: The Victorian elite functioned as a little Gemeinschaft, an intimate community bound by shared culture, memory, status competition and love, atop a large Gesellschaft, and this may have outweighed the opportunity cost of low working hours.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cohesive elite communities may produce coordination benefits that don't show in hours worked.

insights.claim: Folding landed aristocrats, bourgeois and Nonconformists into one British elite, except for Irish Catholics, avoided the hostile counter-elites that produced the American Civil War and strife in Spain, Italy, France and Germany.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Elite unity is a stability factor for political order.

insights.claim: Prestige-based reward let Britain fill unpaid local government roles and Parliament, where candidates bore about £150,000 to £450,000 in election costs in today's money, without difficulty, unlike modern states that struggle to pay public servants competitively.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Status can substitute for pay, but only within a tight community.

insights.claim: Tight membership of one community may have reduced divisiveness and brinkmanship because elites could punish defection from norms, as Bagehot suggested English politicians rarely acted against England's interest.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Norm enforcement by social ties can lower political polarization.
